svg.title: The first line in bladder cancer: Ta, Tis and T1 against T2 and above, and why a registry stage field is not that line
svg.desc: Schematic: Ta, Tis, T1 and T2-and-above on a bladder cancer report are the two sides of one line, drawn in the muscle layer of the bladder wall. The upper half of the figure is a cross-section of the bladder wall in five layers from the inside out. The urothelium, or mucosa, carries Ta, non-invasive papillary carcinoma, and Tis, carcinoma in situ, a flat tumour. The lamina propria, the subepithelial connective tissue, carries T1, tumour invades subepithelial connective tissue. Then comes a thick line labelled "the first line: the muscle layer". Below it the muscle layer, the detrusor, carries T2a, invasion of superficial muscle or inner half, and T2b, invasion of deep muscle or outer half. Outside that the perivesical tissue carries T3a, microscopically, and T3b, macroscopically, an extravesical mass. The outermost layer, adjacent organs, carries T4a, prostate stroma, seminal vesicles, uterus or vagina, and T4b, pelvic wall or abdominal wall. A note under the cross-section records that the UICC TNM 9th edition was published in 2025 but that every bladder column in the official table of changes is marked unchanged, so these definitions are the same in the 8th and 9th editions, and that the Taiwan Cancer Registry report for 2023 states its collapsed stage follows AJCC 8th edition. In the middle are two cards side by side showing what the line decides. The left card, tagged non-muscle-invasive, says that Ta, Tis and T1 can all be treated by transurethral resection and are therefore grouped, for the purposes of treatment, under the heading of non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer; that the guideline adds that this term represents a group definition and that every tumour should still be described by stage, grade and other pathological features, making it a frame drawn to decide treatment rather than a diagnosis; and that which risk group a person falls into, and whether anything is instilled, belongs to another article. The right card, tagged muscle-invasive, says that from T2 upwards a route has to be chosen between removing the bladder and keeping it, and that the grade line is no longer read, because all muscle-invasive urothelial carcinomas of the bladder are high grade and grading therefore provides no prognostic information. Below the two cards a line records that the guideline strongly recommends not using the term "superficial" bladder cancer, the reason given being "because it is incorrect": T1 has already grown into the lamina propria and is not superficial at all. Next comes a panel headed "the stage field in a registry is not this line". At the top is a single full-width stacked bar of the SEER stage field, SEER 21 excluding Illinois, 2016 to 2022: in situ 50 per cent with five-year relative survival 98.0 per cent; localised 34 per cent with 73.0 per cent; regional 7 per cent with 41.8 per cent; distant 6 per cent with 9.6 per cent; unknown 3 per cent. A bracket marks the localised segment and reads: this cell holds T1, with no muscle invasion, and T2, with muscle invaded, at the same time. The note beside it explains that those two groups follow completely different treatment pathways, so a sentence such as "bladder cancer has a five-year survival of 73 per cent" averages the two sides of the line together and amounts to saying nothing; and that for Taiwan no official five-year survival exists at all, because the registry's published survival analysis covers only the ten commonest cancers and bladder cancer is not among them. The Taiwanese distribution follows: the Taiwan Cancer Registry long-form report for year 112, diagnosis year 2023, recorded 3,809 bladder cancers, with collapsed stage by AJCC 8th edition - stage 0 38.08 per cent, stage I 34.68 per cent, stage II 13.06 per cent, stage III 9.37 per cent and stage IV 4.82 per cent - bracketed above as stage 0 plus stage I equals 72.8 per cent, on the left of the line, and stages II to IV equal 27.2 per cent, on the right, over a denominator of 3,737 with a further 72 cases unknown. A note adds that the stage 0 cell must be opened up, because it holds 1,321 cases of Ta and only 102 of Tis. The same panel carries a warning box: Taiwan publishes two official annual counts that are not interchangeable and must never be subtracted from one another - the long-term trend file gives 2,562 cases for 2023, 1,826 men and 736 women, and notes that this is the incidence of invasive cancer, while the long-form report for the same year gives 3,809, including 1,452 carcinomas in situ, 38.1 per cent, alongside 2,357 invasive cancers. Below this is a panel on CIS in two columns. On the left, the guideline definition word for word: an intra-epithelial, high-grade, non-invasive urothelial carcinoma; if it is not biopsied it can be missed at cystoscopy or misinterpreted as an inflammatory lesion; it is often multifocal and can arise in the bladder but also in the upper urinary tract, the prostatic ducts and the urethra; and clinically it comes as primary, secondary or concurrent disease. A red line underneath states that a diagnosis of CIS cannot be made by imaging alone - not CT urography, intravenous urography or ultrasound, and not multiparametric MRI either - so CIS needs a biopsy. On the right, where it puts a person: apart from the very-high-risk group, every patient with CIS falls in the high-risk group; primary CIS alone is high risk; CIS of the prostatic urethra is very high risk. Next, grade written two ways: the left column, the 1973 system, reads G1, G2, G3; the right column, the system from 2004 onwards, reads PUNLMP, low grade, high grade; and the dashed rule between them is labelled to say there is no arrow, no equals sign and no conversion table. The explanation below records that there is a significant shift of patients between the categories of the two systems, the number of high-grade patients under 2004/2022 rising because that category takes in a subset of G2 patients with a better prognosis than G3, and that the panel's systematic review puts it most bluntly: progression rates in G1 patients are similar to those in low-grade patients, while progression rates in G3 patients are higher than in high-grade patients. Then four horizontal bars give five-year progression under the hybrid of the two systems: low grade / G1 1.4 per cent, low grade / G2 3.8 per cent, high grade / G2 7.7 per cent, high grade / G3 18.8 per cent, from 17 centres, 1990 to 2019, 5,145 patients with primary Ta or T1 disease, 64 per cent Ta, median follow-up 3.9 years, log-rank P below 0.001; the C-index for predicting progression is 0.71 for the 1973 system, 0.67 for the 2004 system and 0.73 for the two combined, and neither system predicts recurrence - what they predict is progression. The next panel is the uncertainty in the words themselves, as three bars: agreement on a diagnosis of CIS 70 to 78 per cent; staging T1 against Ta 50 to 60 per cent; reading the grade 50 to 60 per cent. The note says this is not carelessness but a grey zone by nature, and that the guideline therefore adds that in stage T1 and above, or in difficult cases, an additional review by an experienced genitourinary pathologist can be considered. The penultimate panel covers subtypes and lymphovascular invasion: the 2022 World Health Organization classification treats all subtypes as high grade; up to 14.6 per cent of non-muscle-invasive tumours harbour a subtype and more than 5 per cent high-grade component makes it a high-grade tumour; and the features that push a person into the very-high-risk group include pure micropapillary, sarcomatoid, nested, plasmacytoid and neuroendocrine subtypes, along with concurrent CIS, lymphovascular invasion, multiple tumours, residual tumour or an incomplete resection. At the foot of the figure a gold-bordered panel records that of the 3,809 bladder cancers registered in Taiwan in 2023 the 2,357 invasive ones were 95.59 per cent urothelial carcinoma, with 30 neuroendocrine carcinomas, 36 adenocarcinomas and 10 squamous cell carcinomas, and that a different histological type means an entirely different treatment logic; and that the one thing this figure can do is turn the words on the report into questions that can be asked out loud - which T am I and which side of the muscle line does that put me on, which grading system does my report use, does it mention CIS, a subtype or lymphovascular invasion, and is the stage I have been given the clinical one or the pathological one.

g.text: THE LINE IS DRAWN IN THE MUSCLE LAYER
The first line runs through the muscle: Ta, Tis and T1 on
one side, T2 and above on the other
Ta, Tis, T1 and T2 are not a scale of severity. They are the two sides of one line, drawn in the muscle layer of the bladder wall.
What it settles is not "which stage" but which of two entirely different pathways follows.
This figure gives no survival figure without a side to it, and it does not tell you how you should be treated - that is a judgement
your doctor makes from your report, your imaging and your health as a whole. Every number carries its population, its year
and its registry.
The bladder wall from the inside out, and the line
The T definitions below are the TNM definitions as transcribed word for word in the EAU 2026 guideline.
Urothelium (mucosa)
Ta | non-invasive papillary carcinoma
Tis | carcinoma in situ, a "flat tumour"
Lamina propria (subepithelial connective
tissue)
T1 | tumour invades subepithelial connective tissue
The first line: the muscle layer
Muscle layer (detrusor)
T2a | invades superficial muscle (inner half)
T2b | invades deep muscle (outer half)
Perivesical tissue
T3a | microscopically
T3b | macroscopically, an extravesical mass
Adjacent organs
T4a | prostate stroma, seminal vesicles, uterus or vagina
T4b | pelvic wall or abdominal wall
On versions: the UICC TNM 9th edition was published in 2025, but the official table of changes marks every bladder column as unchanged - the definitions above are the same in the 8th and
the 9th editions. The Taiwan Cancer Registry 112 (2023) report states that its collapsed stage follows AJCC 8th edition.
What the line decides
Non-muscle-invasive
Left of the line: Ta, Tis, T1
All of these tumours can be treated by transurethral resection, and
so, for the purposes of treatment, they are grouped under the
heading of non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer.
The guideline adds a sentence of its own: the term represents a
group definition, and every tumour should still be described by its
stage, its grade and its other pathological features. It is a frame
drawn to decide treatment, not a diagnosis.
Which risk group you fall into, and whether anything is instilled into
the bladder, is the subject of another article, "Low, intermediate or
high risk".
Muscle-invasive
Right of the line: T2 and above
A route has to be chosen between removing the bladder and keeping
it; that question is taken up in "Removing the bladder, or keeping it".
The grade line is no longer read. The guideline is blunt: all
muscle-invasive urothelial carcinomas of the bladder are high grade,
and for that reason grading provides no prognostic information.
On the two sides of the line, even which lines of the report matter is
different.
One old word can be dealt with here: the guideline carries a strong recommendation not to use the term "superficial" bladder cancer, and the text gives the reason as
"because it is incorrect". T1 has already grown into the lamina propria; it is not superficial at all.
The stage field in a registry is not this line
This is the cell I see misread most often: registry stage categories and the two lines used in the clinic are two different languages.
The SEER stage field (SEER 21 excluding IL, 2016-2022)
The "localised" cell holds T1 (no muscle invasion) and T2 (muscle invaded) at the same time
In situ 50% | 5-year relative survival 98.0%
Localised 34% | 73.0%
Regional 7% | 41.8%
Distant 6% | 9.6%
Unknown 3%
Those two groups follow completely different treatment pathways. So a sentence like "bladder cancer has a five-year survival of 73%" is not merely imprecise: it
averages the two sides of the line together, which amounts to saying nothing.
For Taiwan there is no equivalent figure at all: the registry's published survival analysis covers only the ten commonest cancers and bladder cancer is not among
them. No official number exists, and this figure quotes no unofficial one.
Which side of the line people in Taiwan are on
Taiwan Cancer Registry long-form report, year 112 (diagnosis year 2023), bladder cancer n=3,809, collapsed stage by AJCC 8th edition
Stage 0 plus stage I = 72.8%
Stages II to IV = 27.2%
Stage I: 34.68%
Stage II: 13.06%
Stage III: 9.37%
Stage IV: 4.82%
Adding up the report's own categories, over a denominator of 3,737 (a further 72 cases are recorded as unknown).
The stage 0 cell has to be opened up, because it holds two very different things: 1,321 cases of Ta and only 102 of Tis, carcinoma in situ.
Taiwan publishes two official annual bladder cancer counts. They are not interchangeable and must never be subtracted from one another
The registry's long-term trend file gives 2,562 bladder cancers for 2023 (1,826 men, 736 women), but the file itself notes that this is the incidence of invasive
cancer.
The long-form report for the same year gives 3,809, which includes 1,452 carcinomas in situ (38.1%) alongside 2,357 invasive cancers.
When you meet a Taiwanese bladder cancer count, the first question is which of the two it is.
CIS is the flat one, and at cystoscopy it often looks like nothing more than inflammation
What it is (the guideline definition, word for word)
An intra-epithelial, high-grade, non-invasive urothelial carcinoma.
If it is not biopsied it can be missed at cystoscopy, or misinterpreted as an
inflammatory lesion.
It is often multifocal, and it can arise in the bladder but also in the upper
urinary tract, the prostatic ducts and the urethra.
Clinically it comes in three forms: primary (no previous and no concurrent
papillary tumour), secondary (found during follow-up after a different tumour)
and concurrent (alongside another urothelial tumour of the bladder).
A diagnosis of CIS cannot be made by imaging alone - not by CT urography,
not by intravenous urography, not by ultrasound, and not by multiparametric
MRI either. CIS needs a biopsy.
Where it puts a person
In the guideline's risk stratification, every patient with CIS falls in the high-risk
group, apart from those in the very-high-risk group.
Primary CIS on its own should be regarded as high risk.
CIS of the prostatic urethra is very high risk.
How those groups decide whether anything is instilled is set out in "Low,
intermediate or high risk", not here.
Grade is written two ways, and the two do not convert into one another
The 1973 system
G1
G2
G3
The system from 2004 onwards (2004 / 2016 / 2022)
PUNLMP
Low grade
High grade
No arrow between them, no equals sign, and no conversion table
The guideline states plainly that there is a significant shift of patients between the categories of the two systems: the number of high-grade patients under 2004/2022
rises, because that category takes in a subset of G2 patients whose prognosis is better than G3.
The panel's own systematic review puts it most bluntly: progression rates in G1 patients are similar to those in low-grade patients, while progression rates in G3
patients are higher than in high-grade patients. G3 is not high grade; the two systems are not measuring quite the same thing.
What can be used is the hybrid of the two, in four steps: five-year progression
Low grade / G1
Low grade / G2
High grade / G2
High grade / G3
17 centres, 1990 to 2019, 5,145 patients with primary Ta or T1 disease (64% Ta, median follow-up 3.9 years), log-rank P<0.001. C-index for predicting progression: 0.71 for the 1973
system, 0.67 for the 2004 system, 0.73 for the two combined. Neither system predicts recurrence; what they predict is progression.
The words on the report carry uncertainty of their own
Agreement on a diagnosis of CIS
Staging T1 against Ta
Reading the grade
This is not carelessness; these particular judgements sit in a grey zone by nature. The guideline therefore adds a sentence: in stage T1 and above, or in difficult cases,
an additional review by an experienced genitourinary pathologist can be considered.
The small print is worth more than the score: subtypes and lymphovascular invasion
The 2022 World Health Organization classification treats all subtypes as high grade.
Up to 14.6% of non-muscle-invasive tumours harbour a subtype, and the percentage of subtype in the specimen should be stated in the report; under the 2022
classification, more than 5% high-grade component makes it a high-grade tumour.
The features that push a person into the very-high-risk group include pure micropapillary, sarcomatoid, nested, plasmacytoid and neuroendocrine subtypes, along
with concurrent CIS, lymphovascular invasion, multiple tumours, residual tumour or an incomplete resection.
This figure does not come to rest on a single number
Of the 3,809 bladder cancers registered in Taiwan in 2023, the 2,357 invasive ones were 95.59% urothelial carcinoma, with 30 neuroendocrine
carcinomas, 36 adenocarcinomas and 10 squamous cell carcinomas - and a different histological type means an entirely different treatment logic. The
one thing this figure can do for you is turn the words on the report into questions you can ask out loud: which T am I, and which side of the muscle line
does that put me on? Which grading system does my report use? Does it mention CIS, a subtype, lymphovascular invasion? Is the stage I have been
given the clinical one or the pathological one?
Schematic, redrawn from the EAU 2026 guidelines on non-muscle-invasive and on muscle-invasive bladder cancer, the UICC TNM 9th edition and its table of
changes (Brierley 2026), van Rhijn 2021, Soukup 2017, the Taiwan Cancer Registry long-form report for 2023 and its long-term trend file, and SEER Cancer Stat
Facts; not reproduced from the figures of the original papers. The cohorts, designs and endpoints of the underlying studies differ, so the data points must not be
compared directly.
